【25】**CASE EXAMPLE 1.5 _Verify Medical Diagnosis_**

【26】A 31-year-old man was referred to physical therapy by an orthopedic physician. The diagnosis was"shoulder-hand syn-drome. This client had been evaluated for this same problem by three other physicians and two physical therapists before arriving at our clinic. Treatment to date had been unsuccessful in alleviating symptoms.

【27】The medical diagnosis itself provided some useful informa-tion about the referring physician. “Shoulder-hand syndrome" is outdated nomenclature previously used to describe reflex sym-pathetic dystrophy syndrome (RSDS or RSD)，now known more accurately as complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS).35，75

【28】Shoulder-hand syndrome was a condition that occurred following a myocardial infarct， or MI (heart attack)， usually after prolonged bed rest. This condition has been significantly reduced in incidence by more up-to-date and aggressive car-diac rehabilitation programs. Today CRPS， primarily affecting the limbs， develops after injury or surgery， but it can still occur as a result of a cerebrovascular accident (CVA) or heart attack.

【29】This client's clinical presentation included none of the typical signs and symptoms expected with CRPS such as skin changes{smooth， shiny， red skin)， hair growth pattem (increased dark hair patches or loss of hair)， temperature changes (increased or decreased)， hyperhidrosis (excessive perspiration)， restricted joint motion， and severe pain. The clinical picture appeared consistent with a trigger point of the latissimus dorsi muscle， and in fact， treatment of the trigger point completely eliminated all symptoms.

【30】**Conducting a thorough physical therapy examination to identify the specific underlying cause of symptomatic presen-tation was essential to the treatment of this case. Treatment approaches for a trigger point differ greatly from intervention protocols for CRPS.**

【31】Accepting the medical diagnosis without performing a physi-cal therapy diagnostic evaluation would have resulted in wasted time and unnecessary charges for this client.

【32】The International Association for the Study of Pain replaced the tem RSDS with CRPS / in 1995.35 Other names given to RSD included neurovascular dystrophy， sympathetic neurovas-cular dystrophy， algodystrophy，“red-hand disease，" Sudeck’s atrophy， and causalgia.

【48】**DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS VERSUS SCREENING**

【49】If you are already familiar with the term differential diagno-sis， you may be wondering about the change in title for this text. Previous editions were entitled Differential Diagnosis in _Physical Therapy._

【50】_The name Differential Diagnosis for Physical Therapists：_ Screening for Referral， first established for the fourth edition of this text， does not reflect a change in the content of the text as much as it reflects a better understanding of the screening process and a more appropriate use of the term “differential diagnosis”to identify and describe the specific movement impairment present (if there is one).

【51】When the first edition of this text was published， the term physical therapy diagnosis was not yet commonly used nomen-clature. Diagnostic labels were primarily within the domain of the physician. Over the years， as our profession has changed and progressed， the concept of diagnosis has evolved.

【52】_A diagnosis by the physical therapist as outlined in the_ Guide describes the patient’s/client's primary dysfunction(s). The diagnostic process begins with the collection of data(examination)， proceeds through the organization and inter-pretation of data (evaluation)， and ends in the application of a label (i.e.， the diagnosis).1

【53】As part of the examination process， the therapist may con-duct a screening examination. This is especially true if the diagnostic process does not yield an identifiable movement dysfunction. Throughout the evaluation process， the thera-pist must ask himself or herself：

【54】.Is this an appropriate physical referral?

【55】Is there a history or cluster of signs and/or symptoms that raises a yellow (cautionary) or red (warning) flag?

【56】The presence of risk factors and yellow or red flags alerts the therapist to the need for a screening examination. Once the screening process is complete and the therapist has con-firmed the client is appropriate for physical therapy interven-tion， then the objective examination continues.

【57】Sometimes in the early presentation， there are no red flags or associated signs and symptoms to suggest an underlying systemic or viscerogenic cause of the client’s NMS symptoms or movement dysfunction.

【58】It is not until the disease progresses that the clinical picture changes enough to raise a red flag. This is why the screening process is not necessarily a one-time evaluation. Screening can take place anywhere along the continuum represented in Fig.删除14:<u>1.4.</u>

【59】The most likely place screening occurs is during the exam-ination when the therapist obtains the history， performs a systems review， and carries out specific tests and measures. It is here that the client presents with constant pain， skin lesions， gastrointestinal problems associated with back pain， digital clubbing， palmar erythema， shoulder pain with stair climbing， or any of the many indicators of systemic disease. Hence in the revised figure in the third edition of the Guide， the pathway for Consultation/Referral is presented after Examination.

【60】The therapist may hear the client relate new onset of symptoms that were not present during the examination. Such new information may come forth anytime during the episode of care. If the patient/client does not progress in physical therapy or presents with a new onset of symptoms previously unreported， the screening process may have to be repeated.

【61】Red-flag signs and symptoms may appear for the first time or develop more fully during the course of physical therapy intervention. In some cases， exercise stresses the client’s phys-iology enough to tip the scales. Previously unnoticed， unrec-ognized， or silent symptoms suddenly present more clearly.

【62】As mentioned， a lack of progress signals the need to con-duct a reexamination or to modify/redirect intervention. The process of reexamination may identify the need for consul-tation with or referral to another health care provider. The medical doctor is the most likely referral recommendation， but referral to a nurse practitioner， physician assistant， chi-ropractor， dentist， psychologist， counselor， a certified or advanced skilled physical therapist， or other appropriate health care professional may be more appropriate at times.

【63】**Scope of Practice**

【64】A key phrase in the APTA standards of practice is “within the scope of physical therapist practice."Establishing a diagno-sis is a professional standard within the scope of a physical therapist’s practice， but may not be permitted according to the therapist’s state practice act (Case Example 1.6).

【65】As we have pointed out repeatedly， an organic problem can masquerade as a mechanical or movement dysfunction. Identification of causative factors or etiology by the physical therapist is important in the screening process. By remaining within the scope of our practice the diagnosis is limited pri-marily to those pathokinesiologic problems associated with faulty biomechanical or neuromuscular action.

【66】When no apparent movement dysfunction， causative fac-tors， or syndrome can be identified， the therapist may treat symptoms as part of an ongoing diagnostic process. Some-times even physicians use physical therapy as a diagnostic tool， observing the client’s response during the episode of care to confirm or rule out medical suspicions.

【68】A licensed physical therapist volunteered at a high school ath-letic event and screened an ankle injury. After performing a heel strike test (negative)， the physical therapist recommended RICE(Rest， Ice， Compression， and Elevation) and follow-up with a medical doctor if the pain persisted.

Always keep in mind that the screening process may， in fact， confirm the presence of a musculoskeletal or neuromuscular problem.

【188】**_Palpation_**

【189】· REGIONAL LYMPH NODES： With patient in sitting position， palpate the axillae and infraclavicular and supraclavicular nodes. This is best done with the patient in a relaxed position. Document any findings， observing for position， mobility， tenderness.

【190】·BREAST EXAMINATION： This should be done initially in the sitting position， support-ing the breast with one hand and examining with the other. The breasts should then be examined with the patient in the supine position， with the arm on the side you are exam-ining above her head. For a woman with large breasts， it may be helpful for her to roll onto the contralateral hip so that you can better palpate the upper and lower lateral quadrants of the breast you are examining and then complete the examination with her on her back.

【191】The entire breast should be examined using a systematic approach： either using small concentric circles with varying degrees of pressure (light， medium， and deep) or the up and down approach also known as the“lawnmower"method. The finger pads should be used for palpation rather than the fingertips. It is important to cover all breast tissue， imagining a rect-angle rather than a circle. Assess for consistency oftissue， presence oftenderness， nodularity， dominant masses， and borders of the mass. Compare asymmetry between breasts.

【1】**Pneumonia**

Pneumonia is one of the commonest causes of pleuritic chest pain. The definition of pneumonia includes symptoms and signs of a respiratory infection and new chest radiographic shadowing consis-tent with consolidation . Supportive features in the history are cough， yellow， green or brown sputum， fever， malaise，|删除表格换行|headache， and a past medical history of conditions predisposing to lower respiratory tract infections， such as COPD， immuno-compromise， or alcoholism. It is important to ask about travel(for Legionella and rarer tropical causes) and any contacts. Breathlessness is usually a feature， but may be less obvious when fit adults with lots of respiratory reserve have a small area of infected lung.

【7】**Pulmonary embolism (PE)**

【8】Pleuritic chest pain with PE is due to pulmonary infarction. This is usually caused by an acute small or medium embolism. Patients classically present with pleuritic chest pain， breathlessness and hae-moptysis. Massive PE may present differently with syncope， central chest pain and severe dyspnoea.

【9】PE should be considered as a possible diagnosis in almost all patients with pleuritic chest pain and is considered one of the most underdiagnosed conditions in acute medicine. Risk fac-tors for PE are listed in Box 10.1. These are usually combined in a pre-test probability score (Wells) to guide further investigation .

【17】**Musculoskeletal chest pain**

【18】Musculoskeletal chest pain is a possibility if there is a history of injury and if the pain appears to be related to movement. This is more difficult to establish than it sounds because movement of the thoracic cage can reproduce pain caused by an inflamed or infected lung. Patients can feel short of breath with musculoskeletal chest pain due to splinting of the chest and anxiety. A history of injury is not always clear， and questions about recent lifting， twisting， and sport are important.

【19】**Exacerbation of asthma or COPD**

【20】Patients with airways disease can develop exacerbations after bacterial or viral lower respiratory tract infections. They will have cough， increased expectoration of sputum， breathlessness and wheeze. The chest radiograph may be normal. Pleuritic pain may be due to co-existent pleurisy or due to musculoskeletal pain from the increased respiration and coughing which accompanies the exacerbation.

【21】**Viral pleurisy**

【22】This is a common cause of pleuritic pain. It is often in the con-text of a viral type illness with upper respiratory tract symptoms， myalgia and fever. There may be either a dry or productive cough. Auscultation may reveal a pleural rub (which can sometimes be felt as well as heard). The chest radiograph is usually normal although occasionally there is a small pleural effusion.

【23】**Pericarditis**

【24】In1pericarditis the pain is typically pleuritic but usually retrosternal and positional. It is worse when lying down and relieved by leaning forward. There may be characteristic ECG changes . The chest radiograph will be normal unless a pericardial effusion causes enlargement of the cardiac silhouette.

【25】**Pneumothorax**

【26】Spontaneouspneumothorax classically causes sudden onset ofpleu-ritic chest pain and breathlessness in a previously healthy patient. The commonest findings are reduced expansion and air-entry on the side of the pneumothorax. The chest radiograph is diagnostic. It usually arises in young， slim males， or in those with COPD，and is sometimes linked to an inherited condition such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

【29】**Case history revisited**

【30】On revisiting the case history the diagnosis is not immediately obvious， and all of the conditions discussed are possible. The most serious diagnosis to consider is pulmonary embolism. The fact that the pain arose outside an immediate context of infective symptoms and is associated with breathlessness means that pulmonary embo-lism still needs to be definitely excluded. There is also exposure to possible hospital acquired infections.

【31】This patient has a significant PE risk factor having had a total hip replacement 2 weeks ago. The swollen leg may represent a deep vein thrombosis (DVT) although after a total hip replace-ment the affected leg will usually be swollen anyway. The wheeze is probably due to COPD； this may be exacer-bated by infection. Wheeze can also sometimes be heard in PE.

【39】There is some chest wall tenderness and musculoskeletal chest pain remains a possibility but this patient has low oxygen satura-tions and an increased respiratory rate indicating lung pathology. 【78】It is always worth asking whether the patient has had vertigo before， and if so， to describe previous episodes. Multiple episodes point towards a diagnosis of Menière's disease， migraine， transient ischaemic attack (TIA) or benign paroxysmal positional vertigo(BPPV)， rather than acute labyrinthitis， or vestibular neuronitis.

【79】**Taking the above into account， and the information provided in this patient's history， the differential diagnosis should include the conditions below.**

【80】**Acute unilateral peripheral vestibulopathy(a.k.a. vestibular neuronitis)**

【81】The cause of this is unknown， but it remains the commonest cause of the first episode of prolonged vertigo. Many different terms are used to describe the syndrome of acute， apparently idiopathic， unilateral vestibular failure but given that the pathology is uncon-firmed， acute peripheral vestibulopathy (APV) would seem the best term. The onset is spontaneous， associated with nausea and vomiting， persisting for more than 24 hours， with ataxic gait， horizontal nystagmus， with the fast phase towards the unaffected ear， and the absence of hearing loss or tinnitus. Ear examination and the Rinne’s and Weber’s tuning fork tests are typically normal.

【82】By definition， APV must last over 24 hours， so at this stage of assessment， it remains in the differential.

【83】**Meniere's disease**

**This is due to episodic increase in pressure of the endolymphatic fluid in the labyrinth and cochlea. The classical presentation is with a prodrome of unilateral aural pressure/fullness， with subsequent onset of vertigo， which lasts several hours and there is associated unilateral deafness and tinnitus， lasting days and sometimes weeks Note that patients may only perceive their hearing loss as a‘blocked|删除1换行|feeling in the ear. Furthermore， as it is usually low frequency loss， it may not be noted at all. Initially there may be episodes of soli-tary vertigo， before the recurrent pattern of vertigo and hearing loss becomes evident over time.

【85】In the typical presentation， one would anticipate a bilateral Rinne's positive (i.e. normal) and Weber's lateralising towards the unaffected side (abnormal).

【86】In this case， the absence of prior episodes and accompanying otological symptoms (aural fullness/pressure， hearing loss and tin-nitus) would be atypical for Menière’s disease， though this attack could be the first episode.

【87】**Focal migraine**

【88】This condition is under-diagnosed and is typified by the complaint of recurrent unprovoked (i.e. not triggered by positional change) vertigo lasting up to around an hour， without hearing loss or tinnitus. A history or family history of any form of migraine， especially focal， would favour this diagnosis. There may be triggers such as menstruation (a drop in oestrogen)， altered sleep pattern， life event ‘stress’ or similar， that triggered the attack.

【89】**As the patient has migraine the diagnosis should be considered， though the duration of the attack would be atypical.**

【133】There are a wide range of reasons why it may be necessary to ask questions about sexual function， birth control， and STDs. For example， joint pain can be caused by STIs. 【134】Whenever taking a sexual history seems appropriate， remember to offer your clients a clear explanation for any questions asked concerning sexual activity， sexual function， or sexual history. 【74】**Mouth-Breathing**

【75】Mouth-breathing is a common observation in pediatric practice. It is responsible for several secondary adverse effects， including dryness of the mouth and lips and their proneness to fissuring and infection.

【76】In a given case， find out if the child mouth-breathes just out of habit or he has an obstructive nasal problem. Does he have persistent or recurrent upper respiratory infection? Does he sneeze a lot?Any headache，hyposmia， or postnasal discharge?

【77】Physical examination should， in particular， exclude adenoids， polyp， foreign body， deviated septum and allergy.

【78】Adenoidal hypertrophy may interfere with the passage of air through the nose， resulting in mouth-breathing， especially during sleep when the child lies supine. When gross adenoidal hypertrophy is present， the child develops a tendency to keep the mouth open during day al-so. Accompanying manifestations may include dryness of the mucous membrane of the mouth and lips， persistent rhinitis， pharyngitis， snor-ing， nasal voice， offensive breath， impaired taste， bad smell， harass-ing cough， impaired hearing and chronic otitis media. Eventually， the child may develop dull expression with open mouth and maloccluded teeth-the so-called adenoid facies. His school performance too suffers.

【79】In a suspected case， digital palpation， indirect visualization with a pharyngeal mirror or fiberoptic bronchoscope， or lateral pharyngeal X-ray may help in clinching the diagnosis.

【90】**1 Introduction**

【91】**On the 18th of June， 1886， at the inaugural meeting of the Association of American Physicians， Dr. Reginald Fitz presented a study titled“Perforating inflammation of the vermiform appendix， with special reference to its early diagnosis and treatment." This study was to be-come a classic in the history of medicine. Fitz was the first to recog-nize that the feared condition previously known as perityphlitis， as well as all its variants， in fact originated from one entity： inflamma-tion of the vermiform appendix. He coined the term “appendicitis”and was the first to advocate early appendectomy as the treatment of choice.**

【92】**In the ensuing years appendectomy became a routine procedure all over the world and the mortality from appendicitis rapidly de-creased. A further decrease in mortality followed the introduction of antibiotics and better anesthetic procedures after World War II.**

【93】**Although appendectomy has been universally accepted as the treatment of choice for appendicitis， the correct diagnosis of this common disease has remained elusive. The diagnosis is as often wrongly made as it is overlooked， the first leading to an unnecessary operation， the second to ill-advised delay. False-positive and false-negative diagnoses both arise at a frequency of approximately 25%and the efforts to improve diagnostic accuracy have been as fruitless as they are countless. Especially in the field of radiology no single di-agnostic method has gained universal acceptance. Diagnosis and therapy still depend largely on history， physical examination， and a few simple laboratory tests.**

【94】**An incidental sonographic finding in a patient in our hospital prompted a study on the value of ultrasound in the diagnosis of ap-pendicitis， the first results of which were published in Radiology in1986. This book reflects a 4-year experience with ultrasound exami-nation in patients with clinical signs of appendicitis.**

【95】**The appendix is the vermiform continuation of the caecum and arises from its posteromedial aspect. It may occupy any position： directed medially (35%)， caudally (30%)， laterally (10%)， or retrocaecally(25%). In the retrocaecal position the appendix may occasionally be situated retroperitoneally. The average length of the appendix is9 cm， and if the lumen is collapsed the average diameter is 4.5 mm. Starting from the lumen， the wall of the appendix  consists of mucosa， submucosa， muscularis， and serosa. The mucosa comprises an epithelial surface and the lamina propria which contains lym-phoid follicles. The muscularis mucosae is often deficient， which ren-ders the transition to the submucosa indistinct. The submucosa is made up of loose connective tissue containing multiple small vessels. Although an immunological role has been suggested， the function of the appendix is still unknown.**

【96】**2.2 Pathophysiology**

【97】**The etiology of acute appendicitis is obstruction， followed by infection. Wangensteen and Dennis (1940) performed experiments with animal appendices， which they ligated at the base after milking some feces from the caecum into the lumen of the appendix. Invariably this procedure resulted in a pathological condition indistinguishable from human appendicitis. He was also able to measure an increase of in-traluminal pressure of an experimentally obstructed human appen-dix. It has been accepted ever since that obstruction is the most im-**

通用删除16(英):<u>**Fig. 2.1. Layers of the appendix wall**</u>|删除换行|portant， probably the only etiological factor precipitating appendici-tis.**

【99】**Whereas the role of obstruction as the main cause of appendicitis is not challenged， the reasons for the obstruction are controversial. It seems hard to clarify this matter since the base of the appendix， which is often the level of obstruction， is inverted into the caecum during the operation and thus not accessible to pathological verifica-tion.**

【100】**It is accepted that in 35% of all patients the presence of a fecolith plays an important role in the pathological process . However， whether the fecolith is the prime originator of the obstruc-tive process or whether it modifies progression after the disease has started is still a matter of speculation. The lamination of most feco-liths clearly indicates that they can be present for a long time without causing any problems. Lymphoid hyperplasia has been implicated as the principal reason for obstruction . This view is sup-ported by the increased incidence of appendicitis observed during outbreaks of measles and mononucleosis . Scar tissue due to previous inflammation may be the precipitating factor in at-tacks of recurrent appendicitis . A functional obstruc-tion， caused by high intraluminal pressure in the caecum - analogous to the pathophysiological mechanism of diverticulitis - has been pro-posed as the main cause of appendicitis. This view is supported by the observation that appendicitis is rare in populations on a high re-sidual diet .**

【101】**Foreign bodies， tumors， parasites， and gall stones are reported as rare causes of obstruction in appendicitis.**

【102】**Bacterial invasion in the absence of obstruction seems unlikely to be the primary etiological agent， since the bacteria found in appendi-citis do not cause small - or large - bowel perforation either unless there is obstruction. There are a few reports on true appendicitis asso-ciated with bacterial enteritis by enteropathogenic microorganisms. However， this is more likely the result of mechanical obstruction of the appendiceal lumen due to the associated hyperplasia of the lym-phoid tissue .**

【103】**A vascular type of appendiceal perforation may exist theoreti-cally， in which the primary lesion is ischemia and not obstruction.**

【104】**Once the appendiceal lumen is obstructed and if the patient is not operated upon soon， there are various pathophysiological path-ways open . In the presence of obstruction continuous mu-cus secretion will cause an increase of the intraluminal pressure and a subsequent stretching of the visceral peritoneum. This is perceived by the patient as visceral pain， localized in the periumbilical or epigastric area. After a while the inflamed serosa touches the parietal perito-neum causing localized pain， responsible for the well-known shift of pain to the right lower abdomen.**

【105】**If at this point the obstruction is relieved spontaneously， appen-dicitis runs an abortive course， and clinical symptoms will rather sud-denly subside.**

【117】**Usually， however， the obstruction persists and the relative inelas-ticity of the appendix soon compromises the lymphatic drainage and blood supply， which renders the appendiceal wall vulnerable to bac-terial invasion. If， at this time， the patient is not operated upon， perfo-ration will occur. If there is free perforation into the abdominal cavi-ty， a spreading and life-threatening peritonitis with formation of distant abscesses will follow. In most cases the spread of pus is con-tained by the omentum， mesentery， bowel loops and adhesions，“walling-off”the perforation. If this protective mechanism functions， a so-called appendiceal mass is formed.**

【118】**If there is merely a phlegmonous mass， the proper name is an ap-pendiceal phlegmon； if there is a circumscribed pus collection within the mass， it is termed an appendiceal abscess. An appendiceal phleg-mon may resolve steadily in the course of weeks， but occasionally a secondary abscess may develop within it. If small， an appendiceal ab-scess may resorb completely. More typically， it will drain spontane-ously into neighboring structures， usually into the bowel， which is the most favorable route， less frequently into the vagina， and rarely into the bladder or through the skin. There is also a chance that the ab-scess will become larger and life threatening： insidious rupture into the circulation may result in septicemia， pylephlebitis or liver ab-scesses， and spilling into the abdominal cavity may cause subsequent generalized peritonitis and formation of distant abscesses.**

【119】**2.3 Epidemiology**

**Although the frequency of appendicitis is decreasing in all industrial-ized Western countries， it is still the most common cause of acute ab-domen . The falling incidence of appen-dicitis has been postulated to result from the inclusion of more fiber|删除1换行|in the diet during the past 20 years. Interestingly there seems to be a rising incidence of appendicitis in persons over 60 years of age . The incidence of appendectomy in Holland was137 per 100000 inhabitants per year in 1985， implying a 9% probabili-ty for a newborn Dutch baby of undergoing appendectomy in the course of a lifetime .**

【121】**At present the average mortality per 1000 appendectomies is 2.2， but the majority of these patients are elderly. The exact mortality from appendicitis is difficult to assess but is not identical to the mor-tality per 1000 appendectomies： patients may die after the removal of a normal appendix or from appendicitis without having the appendix removed， even without an operation at all.**

【122】**Our experience is that the highest mortality is found in elderly patients who are admitted with appendicitis in an advanced stage and are treated conservatively， possibly undergoing abscess drainage but rarely appendectomy. In addition， the diagnosis of appendicitis in the elderly is even more elusive than it is in the general population. Our observations suggest that the mortality from appendicitis， although occurring chiefly in the aged， may actually be higher than statistical data appear to indicate.**

【123】**Late sequelae of appendicitis are cicatricial hernia and small-bowel obstruction due to adhesions.**

【124】**Other rare， but dramatic consequences of appendicitis are fetal death due to appendicitis occurring during pregnancy and tubal in-fertility due to perforated appendicitis or appendiceal abscess. To-gether with the incidental mortality， these sad events are undoubtedly the most feared sequelae of appendicitis for health care nowadays， and they emphasize the importance of diagnostic accuracy and early treatment in young women and in the aged.**

【125】**2.4 Clinical Diagnosis**

【126】**The clinical diagnosis of appendicitis is based on the patient’s his-tory， physical examination and laboratory findings. Radiological examinations are also used， which will be discussed in Sect. 2.10.**

【127】**2.4.1 Patient History**

**The initial symptom in 99.5% of patients with appendicitis is abdomi-nal pain. Classically， the pain starts somewhat diffusely and is experi-enced in the epigastric or periumbilical area. The pain is followed by nausea， incidental vomiting and anorexia. After 6-12 h the nausea subsides， but anorexia frequently persists. After a variable period of time (averaging 6 h)， the pain shifts to the right lower abdomen. This classic sequence， however， is only encountered in two-thirds of pa-|删除1换行|tients and is not uncommon in those with other abdominal condi-tions.**

【129】**When point tenderness develops， it is usually near McBurney's point， but it may occur within a wide radius from this point. If the pain is more diffuse in the lower abdomen， it is useful to let the pa-tient point out where the worst pain is located and where the pain was initially.**

Although cultural competence training has been a part of health care curricula for the past several years， recent stud-ies have shown that there is little evidence that it improves patient outcomes.24 It cannot be denied that there is a need|删除1换行|for better quality research on this topic， but it is also impor-tant to recognize other factors that contribute to widen-ing health disparities and continued inequity in health care access. More recent literature on the social determinants of health attempts to address this topic.

【9】Social determinants of health (SDH) is defined by the World Health Organization as “the conditions in which people are born， grow， work， live， and age， and the wider set of forces and systems shaping the conditions of daily life”.25 Examples of SDH include economic poli-cies and systems， development agendas， social norms， social policies， and political systems.25 Although clinicians are highly encouraged to practice culturally competent delivery of health care， they must also be cognizant of the social deter-minants of health to optimize patient outcomes.

【57】The therapist will use two main interviewing tools during the screening process. The first is the Family/Personal His-tory form . With the client’s responses on this form and/or the client’s chief complaint in hand， the inter-view begins.

【58】The second interviewing tool is the Core Interview . The Core Interview as presented in this chapter provides a guideline for the therapist when asking questions about the present illness and chief complaint. Screening questions may be interspersed throughout the Core Interview， as seems appro-priate and based on each client’s answers to the questions.

【59】There may be times when additional screening ques-tions are asked at the end of the Core Interview or even on a subsequent date at a follow-up appointment.
